passages.quote: To read and interpret piping and instrument drawings (P&IDs), the reader must learn the meaning of the symbols.
The reader should note that this chapter is only representative of fluid system symbology, rather than being all-inclusive.
Valves are used to control the direction, flow rate, and pressure of fluids.
Figure 1 shows the symbols that depict the major valve types.
Some valves are provided with actuators to allow remote operation, to increase mechanical advantage, or both.
Figure 2 shows the symbols for the common valve actuators.
If no actuator is shown on a valve symbol, it may be assumed the valve is equipped only with a handwheel for manual operation.
The combination of a valve and an actuator is commonly called a control valve.
it does not provide enough information to determine how those components react to a control signal.
A positioner is symbolized by a square box on the stem of the control valve actuator.
An additional aspect of some control valves is a valve positioner, which allows more precise control of the valve.
To differentiate between valve uses, a balloon labeling system is used to identify the function of a control valve, as shown in Figure 6.
The common convention is that the first letter used in the valve designator indicates the parameter to be controlled by the valve.
Figure 7 shows commonly used symbols for indicating the medium
Figure 8 shows symbols used to depict pipe fittings.
One of the main purposes of a P&ID is to provide functional information about how instrumentation in a system or piece of equipment interfaces with the system or piece of equipment.
The first three columns above are combined such that the resulting instrument identifier indicates its sensed parameter, the function of the instrument, and the type of instrument.
To create a usable signal, a device must be inserted into the system to detect the desired parameter.
Figure 9 shows the symbols used for the various sensors and detectors.
Figure 10 also illustrates the common notations used to indicate the location of an instrument, i.e., local or board mounted.
Each sensor or detector must be coupled with appropriate modifiers and/or transmitters.
Controllers process the signal from an instrument loop and use it to position or manipulate some other system component.
Note that these types of controllers are also called signal conditioners.
Figure 15 shows the engineering symbols for the most common major components.
Figure 16 lists and explains four of the more common miscellaneous symbols.
Unless otherwise stated, P&IDs indicate valves in their "normal" position.
An exception is safety systems, which are normally shown in their
3-way valves are sometimes drawn in the position that they will fail to instead of always being drawn in their "normal" position.
Figure 17 illustrates the symbols used to indicate valve status.
Fluid power systems are divided into five basic parts: pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines.
Fluid power includes either gas (such as air) or hydraulic (such as water or oil) motive media.
Hydraulic pumps are shown by solid arrow heads.
Pneumatic compressors are represented by hollow arrow heads.
Reservoirs provide a location for storage of the motive media (hydraulic fluid or compressed gas).
An actuator in a fluid power system is any device that converts the hydraulic or pneumatic pressure into mechanical work.
Linear actuators have some form of piston device.
The difference between them is that the point of the arrow touches the circle in a pump and the tail of the arrow touches the circle in a motor.
Rotary actuators are generally called motors and may be fixed or variable.
The sole purpose of piping in a fluid power system is to transport the working media, at pressure, from one point to another.
Valves are the most complicated symbols in fluid power systems.
Fluid power valves, when electrically operated by a solenoid, are drawn in the de-energized position.
Energizing the solenoid will cause the valve to shift to the other port.
When system pressure exceeds its setpoint, the valve opens and returns the hydraulic fluid back to the reservoir.
When PB-1 is pushed and S-1 energized, the 1-2 ports are aligned and 3-4 ports are aligned.
A pictorial diagram shows the physical arrangement of the elements in a system.
A cutaway diagram shows both the physical arrangement and the operation of the different components.
A schematic diagram uses symbols to show the elements in a system.
They do not accurately represent the relative location of the components.

body.text: Facility drafting standards give the symbols used at a site.

body.alt: Chart of valve symbols with alternatives: globe, gate, ball, needle, butterfly, plug, diaphragm, relief, three-way, four-way, check, stop check, angle, rupture disc, and pressure regulator. Most are two triangles meeting point to point on a line.

body.text: Globe and gate valves will often be shown by the same symbol. The valve type may then be given by the component identification number or the notes and legend, but in many cases even those will not say.

checks.q: A P&ID shows a globe valve and a gate valve with the same symbol. Where might the valve type be given?
o: The component identification number or the notes and legend
checks.x: Information on the valve type may be conveyed by the component identification number or the notes and legend, though in many instances even that may not hold true.

checks.q: What are valves used to control?
o: The direction, flow rate, and pressure of fluids
checks.x: Valves are used to control the direction, flow rate, and pressure of fluids.

body.alt: Valve actuator symbols on a valve body: a dome for diaphragm, a box with M for electric motor, a box with S for solenoid, a box with H or a split box for piston, an angled line for reach rod, and a T for manual.

body.text: Each actuator is shown on a gate valve, but an actuator can be attached to any type of valve body.
Control valves are shown by combining the valve symbol and the actuator symbol. Most are controlled manually from a remote station, automatically from an instrument, or both.

body.alt: Air line to a process control valve, with a small solenoid three-way valve in the line that can supply or vent the diaphragm.

body.text: Remote control often uses a small intermediate control valve in the line that supplies motive force to the process control valve. In this example, a solenoid-operated 3-way valve can supply air to the diaphragm or vent it to the atmosphere.
The symbols alone do not show whether air pressure opens or closes the valve, or whether energizing the solenoid pressurizes or vents the diaphragm.

body.alt: Tank with a level controller marked LC, which positions an air-operated diaphragm control valve in the outlet line.

body.text: A control valve run by an instrument is drawn the same way, except the output of the controlling instrument goes to the actuator.

body.alt: Two control valves with a square positioner box on the actuator stem, one with a level controller signal and one with an air supply only.

body.text: The positioner symbol may appear only on detailed diagrams. Larger overall system diagrams may show the same valve as an air-operated valve with no special features.

checks.q: No actuator is shown on a valve symbol. What may be assumed?
o: The valve has only a handwheel for manual operation
The valve is a check valve
checks.x: If no actuator is shown on a valve symbol, it may be assumed the valve is equipped only with a handwheel for manual operation.

checks.q: On a P&ID valve actuator symbol, what does a box with the letter M mean?
checks.x: Figure 2 shows a box marked M on the valve stem for an electric motor actuator. The box marked S is a solenoid.

checks.q: How is a valve positioner symbolized?
o: A circle on the pipe upstream of the valve
A dashed line around the valve
The letters LO beside the valve
A square box on the stem of the control valve actuator
checks.x: A positioner is symbolized by a square box on the stem of the control valve actuator.

checks.q: What is a control valve?
o: The combination of a valve and an actuator
A valve shown in its normal position
A valve with a locked position
checks.x: The combination of a valve and an actuator is commonly called a control valve.

body.text: The second letter is usually a C, which identifies the valve as a controller, or active component. The third letter is a V, which shows the equipment is a valve.

body.alt: Valves with balloons: FCV for flow, TCV for temperature, LCV for level, and PCV for pressure control valve.

checks.q: What does the balloon label PCV mean on a valve?
checks.x: The first letter gives the controlled parameter, C identifies a controller, and V identifies a valve.

body.text: One system's piping may carry more than one medium, and a fluid system diagram may also show instrument signals and electrical wires.

body.alt: Line symbols: solid for process flow, double slashes for pneumatic, a long and short dash or L marks for hydraulic, single slashes for inert gas, dashes for instrument signal, X marks for instrument capillary, and dots or dashes for electrical wires.

body.text: The auxiliary piping symbols identify their mediums, but the process flow line symbol does not.

body.alt: Fitting symbols, including eductor, ejector, pipe reducer, hose connection, screw cap, weld cap, loop seal, atmospheric vent, flexible connection, removable spool, cross, lateral, true Y, blank flange, screwed union, and flange.

body.text: Eductor and ejector symbols are both drawn in the line with a curved upper section and a nozzle shape below.

checks.q: On a P&ID line symbol, what do X marks along the line show?
checks.x: Figure 7 shows X marks along the line for instrument capillary.

checks.q: On a P&ID line symbol, what do pairs of slashes along the line show?
checks.x: Figure 7 shows pairs of slashes for a pneumatic (air) line. Single slashes mark an inert gas line.

checks.q: Which P&ID line symbol does not identify the medium it carries?
checks.x: Although the auxiliary piping symbols identify their mediums, the symbol for the process flow line does not identify its medium.

body.text: Instrument symbols fall into four categories, and each generally uses the identifying scheme in Table 1.

items: Sensed parameter: F flow, T temperature, P pressure, I current, L level, V voltage, Z position
Indicator or controller: R recorder, I indicator, C controller
Component: T transmitter, M modifier, E element
Signal: I current, V voltage, P pneumatic

body.text: The fourth column is used only for a modifier, to show the signals being modified.

checks.q: What does the instrument identifier LIC mean?
checks.x: The letters give the sensed parameter, the function, and the type of instrument. LIC is listed as level indicating controller.

checks.q: What does the instrument identifier TE mean?
checks.x: Table 1 builds TE from T for temperature and E for element.

body.text: In some cases, a device creates special conditions so that another device can supply the measurement.

body.alt: Detector symbols: orifice as two short bars across the line, venturi as two curves, flow element, temperature element with or without a well, thermocouple, rotometer, differential pressure cell, conductivity cell, and radiation detector.

checks.q: On a P&ID, which device is drawn as two curved lines bowing toward the pipe?
checks.x: Figure 9 shows the venturi as two curves on either side of the line. The orifice is drawn as short bars across the line.

body.text: The exceptions are certain local instruments with mechanical readouts, such as bourdon tube pressure gages and bimetallic thermometers.

body.alt: Instrument location symbols: a plain circle for locally mounted, a circle with a solid line across it for board mounted, and a circle with a dashed line for behind the board. Examples of modifiers and transmitters follow.

body.text: A transmitter converts the signal from a sensor or detector to a form that can be sent to a remote point. The output can be electronic (voltage or current), pneumatic, or hydraulic.

A modifier may be identified only by its input and output signals, such as I/P for one that converts an electrical input to a pneumatic output, rather than by the monitored parameter, such as PM for pressure modifier.

body.alt: Examples of indicator and recorder symbols, locally and board mounted, such as FI, TI, FR, TR, and PR balloons.

body.text: Indicators and recorders convert the signal from an instrument loop into a readable form. Like modifiers and transmitters, the symbol shows whether they are locally or board mounted.

checks.q: On a P&ID, what does a circle with a solid line across it mean?
checks.x: Figure 10 shows a plain circle for a locally mounted instrument, a solid line across the circle for board mounted, and a dashed line for behind the board.

checks.q: What does a modifier marked I/P do?
o: Converts an electrical input to a pneumatic output
Converts a pneumatic input to an electrical output
checks.x: Modifiers may be identified by input and output signal, such as I/P for one that converts an electrical input to a pneumatic output.

checks.q: Which instruments do not need a modifier or transmitter?
o: Certain local instruments with mechanical readouts
checks.x: The exceptions are certain types of local instrumentation having mechanical readouts, such as bourdon tube pressure gages and bimetallic thermometers.

body.text: Controllers are generally shown by placing a C in the balloon after the controlling parameter.

body.alt: Balloons marked FC, TC, PC, and LC for flow, temperature, pressure, and level controllers.
Balloons marked P for proportional, PI for proportional-integral, PID for proportional-integral-differential, and I/P for current to pneumatic.

body.text: Figure 10 shows a square root extractor as a circle or square holding a square root sign.

body.alt: Two instrument loops. A: a temperature transmitter feeds a recorder and a PID controller, then an I/P modifier and a valve. B: a tank level transmitter feeds a level modifier, a recorder, and a level control valve.

body.text: In Figure 14 (A), a temperature transmitter sends one signal to a board-mounted recorder and one to a PID controller. An I/P modifier converts the controller output to a pneumatic signal, commonly 3 psi to 15 psi, which operates the valve. The loop modifies flow based on process fluid temperature.
In Figure 14 (B), a pneumatic level transmitter feeds a board-mounted level modifier, which drives a recorder and sends a modified pneumatic signal to the level control valve.
Neither loop shows how the sensed value and the valve are related. Knowing the setpoint and the purpose of the system will usually be enough to work out how the loop operates.

checks.q: Which symbol marks a proportional-integral-differential controller?
checks.x: Figure 13 shows P, PI, and PID balloons for the three controllers. I/P is current to pneumatic.

checks.q: What is another name for proportional, proportional-integral, and proportional-integral-differential controllers on a P&ID?
checks.x: These types of controllers are also called signal conditioners.

checks.q: How is a controller generally denoted in an instrument balloon?
o: A C after the controlling parameter
A T after the controlling parameter
A dashed line across the balloon
checks.x: Controllers are generally denoted by placing a C in the balloon after the controlling parameter.

body.alt: Component symbols with alternatives: centrifugal pump, positive displacement pump, heat exchanger, compressor, fan, tank, and strainer.
Flags marked with a drawing number and grid coordinate, pointing out, in, or both ways, plus a dashed building or area boundary line.

body.text: Pipe or wire continuation flags give the other drawing and its grid coordinates. The flag shape shows whether flow is to that drawing, from that drawing, or in both directions.

checks.q: What does a P&ID continuation flag give the reader?
o: The other drawing number and grid coordinates
checks.x: Figure 16 shows that the symbol gives the drawing number, the grid coordinate, and the flow direction.

body.text: The reader must be able to determine the valve position, know if it is normal, know how the valve will fail, and in some cases know if it is normally locked in that position.

body.alt: Valve status symbols: closed is solid black, open is outlined, throttled is half solid, LO locked open, LC locked closed, FO fails open, FC fails closed, FAI fails as is, and a three-way valve with the closed port solid.

items: Three-way valve: the closed port is filled
Locked open: LO; locked closed: LC
Fails open: FO; fails closed: FC; fails as is: FAI

body.text: This is usually taken as the normal or primary flowpath for the system. Safety systems are the exception, and are normally shown in their standby or non-accident condition.
This will be defined as the standard for the system of drawings or noted on the drawing.

checks.q: How is a closed valve shown on a P&ID?
o: With the valve symbol filled solid
checks.x: Figure 17 shows the closed valve filled solid. An open valve is outlined and a throttled valve has one half filled.

checks.q: What marking shows a locked-closed valve on a P&ID?
checks.x: Figure 17 shows LC under a solid valve for locked closed.

checks.q: In what condition are safety systems normally shown on a P&ID?
checks.x: An exception to the normal position rule is safety systems, which are normally shown in their standby or non-accident condition.

body.text: Fluid power diagrams use a different set of symbols, though some match or resemble those on P&IDs.
The basic pump symbol is a circle with one or more arrow heads showing the flow direction, with the points of the arrows touching the circle.

body.cap: Fluid Power Pump and Compressor Symbols
body.alt: Circles with arrowheads touching the rim: a fixed displacement pump with a solid arrowhead, a variable displacement pump with a diagonal arrow through the circle, and a compressor with a hollow arrowhead.

body.text: Pneumatic reservoirs are usually simple tanks, drawn as a variation of a cylinder. Hydraulic reservoirs can be more complex, so their symbols show how fluid is admitted and removed.

body.alt: Reservoir symbols: open, pressurized, and with connecting lines above or below the fluid level for hydraulic systems, and an oblong tank for air or gases.

checks.q: On a fluid power drawing, how is a compressor told apart from a hydraulic pump?
o: A compressor has hollow arrow heads
A compressor has solid arrow heads
A compressor has a square symbol
checks.x: Hydraulic pumps are shown by solid arrow heads. Pneumatic compressors are represented by hollow arrow heads.

checks.q: What are the five basic parts of a fluid power system?
o: Pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines
Pumps, motors, tanks, filters, and gages
Sensors, transmitters, modifiers, controllers, and valves
Compressors, accumulators, heaters, fans, and strainers
checks.x: Fluid power systems are divided into five basic parts: pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines.

body.text: Actuators are classified as linear or rotary.

body.alt: Single-acting and double-acting cylinders, each shown as a pictorial, a force illustration, and a drawing symbol.
Rotary motor symbols for fixed displacement, variable displacement, and oscillating motors, with the arrow tails touching the circle.

Fluid power line symbols: working, pilot, drain, flexible, joining, and crossing lines, connectors, flow direction, vented manifold, plugged connection, test station, power takeoff, restrictions, and strainer.

checks.q: How does the symbol for a rotary motor differ from the symbol for a pump?
o: In a motor, the tail of the arrow touches the circle
In a motor, the point of the arrow touches the circle
A motor is drawn as a square
checks.x: The point of the arrow touches the circle in a pump and the tail of the arrow touches the circle in a motor.

checks.q: What does an actuator do in a fluid power system?
o: Converts hydraulic or pneumatic pressure into mechanical work
checks.x: An actuator is any device that converts the hydraulic or pneumatic pressure into mechanical work.

body.text: A fluid power valve commonly has three to eight pipes attached and can route one or more fluids in many combinations, so its symbol must hold more information than a standard P&ID valve.

body.alt: Cutaway of a four-way, three-position valve, with the flow shown in each of three positions.
Five steps to build a valve symbol: start with a box, add ports, show the flow in each position in its own box, add the actuating mechanism, then combine them.
Chart of fluid power valve symbols: check, manual shutoff, maximum pressure relief, single and multiple flow path boxes, and directional valves with two or three positions.

body.text: If the valve is operated by something other than a solenoid or is a multiport valve, the information needed will be on the drawing or its legend print.

checks.q: In what position are solenoid-operated fluid power valves drawn?
checks.x: Fluid power valves, when electrically operated by a solenoid, are drawn in the de-energized position.

body.alt: Hand pump on a well, with a hose running to a nozzle.

body.cap: Line Diagram of Simple Hydraulic Power System
body.alt: Legend of symbols for the hand pump system, and the same system as a fluid power line diagram.

body.text: Each part of a simple system can be listed with its symbol and redrawn as a fluid power diagram.

body.alt: Press circuit: an open reservoir with a strainer feeds a motor-driven pump, a relief valve with a gage, a four-way two-position valve with solenoid S-1 and pushbutton PB-1, and a cylinder.

body.text: First get an overall view. In this diagram, the arrows between A and B show the system presses or clamps a part between two sections of the machine.

items: Area 1: open reservoir with a strainer that cleans the oil
Area 2: fixed displacement pump, electrically operated
Area 3: spring-operated relief valve with a separate pressure gage

body.text: As drawn, high pressure fluid goes from Port 1 to Port 3 and to the bottom chamber, which holds the piston retracted. When the piston is fully retracted, the relief valve lifts and holds system pressure at setpoint.
Fluid then enters the top chamber and drives the piston down, while the bottom chamber drains through ports 3-4 to the reservoir. The piston travels until PB-1 is released or full travel is reached.

checks.q: In the press circuit, what happens when PB-1 is pushed and S-1 is energized?
o: Fluid enters the top chamber and drives the piston down
Fluid enters the bottom chamber and retracts the piston
checks.x: With ports 1-2 and 3-4 aligned, fluid enters the top chamber and drives the piston down while the bottom chamber drains to the reservoir.

checks.q: What does the relief valve do when system pressure exceeds its setpoint?
o: Vents the fluid to the atmosphere
Opens and returns hydraulic fluid to the reservoir
checks.x: When system pressure exceeds its setpoint, the valve opens and returns the hydraulic fluid back to the reservoir.

body.text: Pictorial diagrams show outlines of each item, not internal function, and are not especially valuable for maintenance or troubleshooting.

body.alt: Pictorial fluid power diagram with a parts list: reservoir, electric motor, pump, relief valve, directional valve, flow control valve, check valve, and cylinder.

body.text: Cutaway diagrams are generally used for instruction. They need so much space that they are not usually used for complicated systems.

body.alt: The same system as a cutaway diagram, with the internal parts of each component visible.

body.text: Schematics supply the functional information of the system, and are useful in maintenance and troubleshooting.

body.alt: The same system as a schematic diagram, using only fluid power symbols.

checks.q: Which fluid power diagram type is most useful for troubleshooting?
checks.x: Schematics are useful in maintenance work, and understanding them is an important part of troubleshooting. Pictorial diagrams are not especially valuable for this.

examples.title: Identify components on a P&ID

fig.alt: Exercise P&ID: tank E feeds pumps A and B through motor valves 2 and 3. Two trains run through check, motor, and air-operated valves, with heat exchangers C and D, to outlets F, G, H, and I. Valves 18 and 19 are locked-closed cross-connects.

examples.problem: Using the exercise P&ID, identify a centrifugal pump, a heat exchanger, the tank, the venturi, the rupture disc, a relief valve, and the current-to-pneumatic converter.
steps: Pumps are drawn as circles with a tangent outlet: A and B.
Heat exchangers are circles with a zigzag tube: C and D.
The tank is E, the venturi is 31, and the rupture disc is 1.
Relief valves are 8 and 17. The I/P box is 28.
examples.answer: Pump A or B, heat exchanger C or D, tank E, venturi 31, rupture disc 1, relief valve 8 or 17, converter 28.

examples.title: Read valve types and status
examples.problem: On the same P&ID, identify the motor-operated valves, the air-operated valves, the check valves, the solenoid valves, and the locked valves.
steps: A box marked M on the stem is a motor operator: 2, 3, 7, and 16.
A dome on the stem is an air-operated diaphragm: 10 and 21.
Check valves are 5 and 14. Solenoid valves are 11 and 23.
Solid valves marked LC are locked closed: 18 and 19. Valve 4 is marked LO.
examples.answer: Motor 2, 3, 7, 16; air 10, 21; check 5, 14; solenoid 11, 23; locked closed 18, 19; locked open 4.

examples.title: Find the controlling parameter
examples.problem: What is the controlling parameter for Valves 10 and 21?
steps: Trace the signal back from each valve's diaphragm to the I/P modifier.
Follow the dashed signal lines from the modifier to the elements marked TE.
examples.answer: Temperature, as sensed by the temperature elements (TE).

examples.title: Set a valve lineup
examples.problem: Which valves must change position for Pump B to supply flow to only points G and H?
steps: Pump B must reach the upper train, so a closed cross-connect has to open.
Flow to outlets F and I must be stopped at their outlet valves.

examples.title: Read the failure modes
examples.problem: Which valves fail open, fail closed, and fail as is?
steps: Look for the FO, FC, and FAI marks next to each valve.
examples.answer: Fail open: 2 and 3. Fail closed: 10 and 21. Fail as is: 7 and 16.

facts.q: What does the first letter of a control valve designator show?
facts.a: The parameter to be controlled by the valve: F flow, T temperature, L level, P pressure, or H hand.

facts.q: What may be assumed if no actuator is shown on a valve symbol?
facts.a: The valve is equipped only with a handwheel for manual operation.

facts.q: How does a P&ID show where an instrument is mounted?
facts.a: A plain circle is locally mounted, a solid line across the circle is board mounted, and a dashed line is behind the board.

facts.q: How does a fluid power drawing tell a pump from a motor?
facts.a: The point of the arrow touches the circle in a pump. The tail of the arrow touches the circle in a motor.

facts.q: How does a fluid power drawing tell a hydraulic pump from a compressor?
facts.a: Hydraulic pumps have solid arrow heads. Pneumatic compressors have hollow arrow heads.

facts.q: How are safety systems normally shown on a P&ID?
facts.a: In their standby or non-accident condition.

facts.q: In what position are solenoid-operated fluid power valves drawn?
What are the three types of fluid power diagrams?

summary.text: This chapter reviewed the common P&ID symbols for valves, valve operators, process piping, instrumentation, and common system components.
P&IDs show valves in their normal position unless otherwise stated, with symbols for valve condition and failure mode.
Reading a P&ID means identifying the components, then working out the flowpath for a given valve lineup.
Fluid power diagrams use their own symbols for pumps, reservoirs, actuators, valves, and lines.
Pictorial, cutaway, and schematic diagrams all show fluid power systems, and schematics give the functional information.
